name: Hydrogen peroxide gum rinse
lead: A hydrogen peroxide gum rinse is a diluted solution of hydrogen peroxide swished in the mouth as an antiseptic. People use it for healthier-looking pink gums, a cleaner mouth and, some say, brighter-looking teeth, which all feed into how a smile looks. Hydrogen peroxide is also the active agent in many tooth-whitening products [1][3].

A review summarised on Wikipedia found a positive effect of dilute hydrogen peroxide over placebo for gingivitis and plaque, but concluded that chlorhexidine is far more effective [1]. Gingivitis articles list hydrogen peroxide among antiseptic rinses used for prevention and home treatment [2]. Wikipedia's mouthwash article describes peroxide as an oxidising rinse, such as a 1.5% product, often used short-term for acute necrotising ulcerative gingivitis, that kills anaerobic bacteria and froths against debris [4].

Forum users describe long-term peroxide rinsing and report cleaner checkups and whiter-looking teeth, while dental authorities note that prolonged use can cause side effects such as enlarged papillae on the tongue [4][5].
infobox: Healthier gums, cleaner and brighter smile

paras: The cited review found hydrogen peroxide beneficial over placebo for plaque and gingivitis but much less effective than chlorhexidine.[1] A 2004 randomised trial supported a fluoridated hydrogen peroxide rinse for gingivitis.[2]

Peroxide whitens teeth by diffusing into the tooth and breaking down into free radicals that split pigment molecules into smaller, less pigmented pieces, so less light is absorbed [3]. Whitening gels are far more concentrated than a rinse: in-office gels typically hold 10-44% carbamide peroxide, roughly 3-16% hydrogen peroxide, and the EU limits retail products to 0.1% hydrogen peroxide, with up to 6% allowed under dental supervision [3]. Sensitivity is common after in-office whitening, and peroxide at 10% or higher can damage gum tissue, with poorly fitting trays a common cause of chemical burns [3].
Concentrations as low as 3% can be dangerous to the eye.[1] The FDA generally recognises hydrogen peroxide as safe as an antimicrobial agent, though this is not specific to dental use.[1]
Wikipedia's mouthwash article reports that side effects can occur with prolonged use, including hypertrophy of the lingual papillae [4].

A systematic review found hydrogen peroxide rinses better than placebo for gingivitis and plaque but less effective than chlorhexidine,[1] and a 2004 randomised trial supported a fluoridated hydrogen peroxide rinse.[2]

lore.intro: Peroxide mouthwash appears on T Nation as a long-running habit among lifters and as an alternative to prescription chlorhexidine.

claims.claim: A peroxide rinse calms inflamed gums and keeps plaque down.
claims.believers: Proponents say its antiseptic action reduces gum bacteria cheaply; one T Nation poster says gums stay healthy and cleanings need very little [5].
claims.experts: A review found benefit over placebo but chlorhexidine more effective [1].

claims.believers: A T Nation poster says people began asking if he had whitened his teeth after he started rinsing [5].
claims.experts: Peroxide is the active agent in whitening products, but those use much higher concentrations under regulation [3].

claims.claim: Peroxide can stand in for prescription mouthwash.
claims.believers: A poster who asked about chlorhexidine says he has used peroxide mouthwash for years [6].
claims.experts: The review reports chlorhexidine is far more effective than peroxide [1].

card.summary: Dilute peroxide swished as a gum antiseptic; some trial support for gingivitis but chlorhexidine is reported more effective.

quick.overview:
A hydrogen peroxide rinse is a diluted solution swished in the mouth to reduce plaque and gum inflammation.

A review found it better than placebo for gingivitis but far less effective than chlorhexidine.
quick.mechanism: It acts as an antimicrobial and oxidising agent on oral bacteria and plaque.
quick.risks: Even 3% solutions can injure the eye; the FDA generally recognises peroxide as safe as an antimicrobial, not specifically for dental use.

chain: Peroxide rinse kills anaerobic bacteria and loosens plaque
Healthier-looking gums and a cleaner, brighter smile
angle.text: People swish dilute peroxide to keep gums pink and calm and to keep plaque down; some also say it makes teeth look whiter, since peroxide is the active agent in whitening products.
